questions.question: Explain why Allied prisoners of war were treated so harshly by Japan.
questions.expected_answer: Japanese military ideology (Bushido as promoted by the militarist state, 1941 Field Service Code) taught that surrender was shameful, so prisoners were despised. Japan signed but did not ratify the 1929 Geneva Convention and in practice ignored it, using prisoners for forced labour and denying food, medicine and Red Cross access. Brutal internal discipline was passed down to prisoners; many guards were mistreated Korean and Taiwanese conscripts. Racism on both sides, few Japanese POWs in Allied hands, tropical disease and wartime shortages added to the toll: about 27 per cent died versus about 4 per cent held by Germany and Italy.

questions.question: Describe the conditions faced by prisoners, with reference to Bataan, Changi and the hell ships.
questions.expected_answer: Bataan, April 1942: about 76 000 starving American and Filipino prisoners marched about 100 km in heat; stragglers were beaten or killed and thousands died. Changi, Singapore: prisoners organised gardens, hospital, lectures and concerts but suffered starvation diseases (beriberi, pellagra); beatings for not bowing, executions for escape. Hell ships: unmarked cargo ships with prisoners crammed in holds; some sunk by Allied submarines, e.g. Montevideo Maru, 1 July 1942, about 1 000 Australians. Sandakan marches 1945: only six of about 2 400 survived.

questions.question: Describe the building of the Burma-Thailand Railway and explain its human cost.
questions.expected_answer: Japan needed a 415 km supply railway from Ban Pong (Thailand) to Thanbyuzayat (Burma); surveyed at five years, it was completed in about sixteen months (October 1943). About 60 000 Allied prisoners and over 200 000 Asian romusha worked mostly by hand, e.g. at Hellfire Pass, through the 1943 speedo and monsoon. Starvation rations, cholera, dysentery, malaria and ulcers killed about 12 000 to 13 000 prisoners and 80 000 to 100 000 Asian labourers, who are often forgotten.
